utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Would the Registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-5/18-R77.2, in the contempt case of Milan Tupajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Aleksandar Lazarevic, and I will represent Mr. Tupajic in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Good morning, Mr. Tupajic. Are you following the proceedings in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can follow the proceedings without any difficulties. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we begin today, the Chamber will give a summary of the case against the accused, Mr. Milan Tupajic. On the 9th of September, 2011, the Prosecution filed a motion to the Chamber in the Karadzic case seeking a subpoena to compel the testimony of Witness Milan Tupajic. On the 23rd of September, 2011, the Chamber in that case issued a subpoena ordering Mr. Tupajic to appear and testify in the Karadzic case on the 3rd of October, 2011. On the 5th of October, 2011, the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina filed a Memorandum of Service which indicated correspondence from Mr. Tupajic indicating that he was unwilling to appear and testify in the Karadzic case. On the 3rd of November, 2011, the Chamber in the Karadzic case issued a second subpoena again ordering Mr. Tupajic to testify in the Karadzic case. On the 8th of November, 2011, the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina filed a Memorandum of Service which indicated that Mr. Tupajic refused to comply with the second subpoena. As recalled earlier, Mr. Tupajic is being prosecuted for contempt for having knowingly and willingly interfered with the administration of justice by refusing to comply with two subpoenas ad testificandum. Now, Mr. Lazarevic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In this case, Mr. Tupajic after consulting his Defence decided to testify by himself in his defence. We intend to admit -- well, to offer for admittance 20 documents which will corroborate Mr. Tupajic's testimony and that's basically all that we have, and we believe that his testimony will be completed today by the end of working hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So please proceed, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will now call Mr. Tupajic to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would Mr. Tupajic take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tupajic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may just for a second use Mr. Usher's assistance. For Mr. Tupajic's convenience, I made hard copies of all the documents that I intend to use. I believe that it would be much easier for him to deal with hard copies, and I have one binder if I could hand it over to Mr. Tupajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. By all means, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Tupajic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Before we commence with your evidence, I'd like to caution you about one thing. I know that you've already testified before this Tribunal. Still, since both of us speak the same language, wait for me to put my question fully and wait for it to be recorded in the transcript, which will be indicated by the cursor stopping on the screen, and then proceed with your answer. This is to ensure that all your answer -- answers are accurately recorded.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will do my best to assist in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let us begin with some of -- information concerning your personal background, starting with your full name.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: My name is Milan Tupajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 2nd of June, 1954, in the place called Knezina in the municipality of Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And where do you reside at present?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: In Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have -- I have been married since 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, two sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And what are their ages?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: The older son is 30, and the younger 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any grandchildren?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, do you have any employment at present? Can you tell Their Honours?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: No. I have not been employed since 30 -- 30th June 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So where do you earn your livelihood?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Well, from that date until the month of April of 2006, I didn't have any earnings, whereas in April of 2006, a commission of the Republika Srpska PIA fund declared that I should be retired, and I have been retired ever since.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It seems, therefore, that you have retired at a rather early age. What was the reason for your retirement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Well, I was retired early because in June of 2004, I had a very serious heart condition which worsened over time. In April of 2006, the situation exacerbated and the commission decided that I am 70 per cent disabled. Since that moment, I have been retired as a disabled person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will get back to that at some point during your evidence. I just wanted Their Honours to know where you get your earnings from. Can you tell us what is your pension at present.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: In 2006, it was 180 euros, and at present it is 290 euros.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: A couple of more questions concerning your family situation. Does your spouse have an employment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: She did have until last August, August of last year. Unfortunately, she was declared redundant and was dismissed. So in our family of four, formally nobody is employed save for my older son who occasionally does an odd job, though I must say it's on the black market, whereas -- although he had graduated two and a half years ago from the faculty of transport, and my younger son is still studying. So we are having it pretty hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we now have a clear picture of your family situation. Can you tell us if your wife has managed to become retired in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: No. She's currently registered with the unemployment agency. That's the standard procedure, and she is entitled to some 200 euros of unemployment benefit in the coming four or five months, and at the end of that period, we will be down to my pension. And, of course, given the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, although I have a degree in economics and -- although she has a degree in economics and has been working for 28 years in her profession, it will still be very difficult for her to find a new job.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tupajic. A couple of more questions before we move on. Can you tell us first if you have served your military service and when.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. From mid-1979 to mid-1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you get any sort of rank during your military service or any sort of decoration?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: No. I have a degree in mechanical engineering and my line of profession is motor vehicle. It was in Vojvodina in Serbia that I served my military service, and I was trained in driving, basically. And after having done my compulsory training, I assisted my instructors in teaching people driving. I was only given a medal for exemplary conduct, for being a model soldier, and that was a credit for -- that was the credit for my proper service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: One last question on this score. Do you have any misdemeanour or criminal record, and, if so, what sort?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: No. This is the first time that I am appearing before a court of law, whatever branch of law it may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, let us move to a different topic now. It has to do with your experience with this Tribunal so far and your dealings with it. Can you tell Their Honours how far back was your first contact with the Tribunal? And when I say "the Tribunal," I mean any part of it, including the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: The first contact I had with the ICTY OTP was in December of 2002 in Banja Luka. The interview lasted the whole day. This was followed by a number of contacts. Should I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me guide you with my questions to make sure that everything is properly recorded and understood. So in December of 2002, you were first approached by the ICTY OTP. Can you tell us what sort of contact was it? Was it by telephone or in writing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: It was a telephone call. As I said, at the time I was a deputy of the National Assembly. The seat of the National Assembly was and is still in Banja Luka. Since the National Assembly was in session at the time, I suggested that my meeting with them take place in Banja Luka, and that was how it happened. We -- I mean the Assembly was in session for two or three days, and we met, the Prosecution and I, in Banja Luka at what I believe to be a UN base.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You say that this first conversation or interview you had with them was that day. How long did it last?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Well, some six to seven hours in substance, and if you count in the breaks, perhaps a bit longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement for the OTP at the time in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: No. I have never given the standard statement to the Prosecution. This was merely a conversation between me and representatives of the Prosecution. The interview was recorded and there is a transcript to that effect. I have never been given an opportunity to sign any sort of statements either in relation to that first interview or to those that followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But at any rate, you have already told us that those -- that the interview was taped, and let me ask you what you spoke about.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: We spoke about the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but more about the events in the Sokolac municipality and the wider area in 1991 until the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. After that first interview in 2002 in Banja Luka, did you ever meet with the OTP of this Tribunal again, and did you speak to them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 2003. I cannot exactly remember the date, not even the month, although I had my passport on me, although it's expired now, and it has all the entry stamps of my travels here. I was summoned by Mr. Tieger, who explained to me that his investigators doesn't have enough time to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina and asked me whether I was willing to come to The Hague to continue the talks with them. I must admit it was not so easy for me to come, because that was the first time I ever came here, especially on my own, but I did respond to all three invitations, which means that in April 2003, I was in The Hague three times and spoke to OTP representatives for a couple of days in a row each time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In that period, and I mean 2002/2003, did you ever refuse to meet OTP representatives and talk to them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Never during these almost ten years did I refuse any initiative from the ICTY until that subpoena, unfortunately, which came in. And it wasn't easy for me to bear, because that was the first time I have ever failed to respond to an official summons of an official institution, but I will later try to explain how that happened, and I'll try to convince this Trial Chamber that I had valid reasons for doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Yes, we'll get there yet, but while we're dealing with this topic, tell us whether you have already testified before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I testified in late June 2005 in the Krajisnik trial. I was an OTP witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to go into the details of your testimony. What matters to me is that you tell us to what extent you testified. As far as you remember, how much time -- how long before the testimony did you come to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I arrived some three or four days in advance. There is a period for proofing and preparing witnesses, as far as I know, and that stage of preparation for the testimony may have taken as much time, but I'm sure there are records about that. I think I may have been three days -- or may have arrived three days prior to my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your testimony itself, how long did that take from the moment you made the solemn declaration till the moment when you were released?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I think that it went on for some two and a half days. I think that on the last day we began in the morning and we finished around noon. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And that was a full examination, that is, an examination-in-chief followed possibly by a cross-examination and maybe a re-examination. That is, you underwent all the stages of a witness examination.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the procedure that I had been able to observe following the trials here on TV and otherwise. There was nothing special about the procedure. It was all standard procedure when you examine witnesses here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you testify in public session or possibly private or closed session?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I testified in open session, although Mr. Tieger asked me if I wanted or preferred to testify in closed session or under protective measures, but I declined that, because never in my life have I done anything secretly. Whatever I did, I did openly and transparently. And I still stand by everything I said during that testimony, and I also stand by the approximately 70 hours of interviews that were taped before that. I saw it as my duty to try to give a contribution to establishing the truth about the events in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I thought that would be the end of my duties towards this Tribunal, because I had said what was most important and everything that I was asked to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this rather detailed answer. There are some details, though, I would like to ask you about as they may prove important for your subsequent examination. Are you familiar with the full scope of protective measures this Tribunal can offer to witnesses who have such needs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am fully familiar with that, and I must point out that Mr. Tieger and his co-workers were very fair in all their contacts with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I only have a couple more questions about your relations with the Tribunal. Did you have a political function in the RS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but before that I would like to explain how that came about. As I have already said, I'm a mechanical engineer by training. After graduating from university, I worked at the Fabrika Motora in Sarajevo [Realtime transcript read in error "Srebrenica"]. Once a ball bearing factory was built in my hometown of Sokolac by a Swedish firm, the local leadership contacted me and asked me if I could help in the implementation of that project, and I worked there until June 1991, when unfortunately that factory ceased to operate. Then I was contacted by some people from the party that was in power then, because the position of president of municipality had been vacated, and I became president of the municipality from 20 -- from 1 August 1991 until 7 November 1997. At the first elections after the civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina in late 1996, I was also elected a deputy, and I remained deputy until 29 June 2004, when I was removed from office pursuant to the decision of the High Representative, Mr. Ashdown.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, but please wait for a moment for the sake of the record, because I --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may correct the transcript, it's on page 11, row 7, it says here "Srebrenica." Instead of that it should read "Sokolac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. That will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, let me now go back to the part of your evidence where you said that you were a deputy in the Assembly of the Republika Srpska. I would like the Trial Chamber to get a complete picture of that. Please tell us which party delegated you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I was a deputy of the Serbian Democratic Party, and from 1998 to 2004, I was also chairman of the caucus of the SDS and the National Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: While you were both deputy and chairman of the SDS caucus in the National Assembly of Republika Srpska, was the topic of co-operation with the ICTY on the agenda of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember, in 2000 the National Assembly of Republika Srpska adopted a law on the co-operation with the ICTY, but there were problems, and there was obstruction in the process of passing that law, not only among the deputies from my party but also other parties. Then and much earlier, too, not to mention the present time, I was aware of the fact that such a law must be passed, because it's -- it doesn't only serve the interests of the ICTY but also the interests of the RS. I believe that my authority may have been decisive in the adoption of that law. As we were the majority in parliament then, it wouldn't have been possible to adopt that law without our support. There were some deputies who were against that, and they voted against that law. That's when I became aware that these matters need to be taken care of. By the way, all my life I had been a legalist, and I've always tried to -- I've always striven to -- for my activities to be in the framework of the law. And if I may add that my interventions must have been recorded in the transcripts from the National Assembly sessions. The minister of justice was Biljana Maric then, and the prime minister was Mr. Ivanic in 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let us now take a look at a document that has to be -- has to do with what you have just spoken about. That's document D20. In the binder you have in front of you, that's the last document. It's at the W tab. As we see in the upper right-hand corner of this document, it is addressed to the Office of the High Representative for Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let me first ask you if this is your handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What were the circumstances of the drafting of this letter? When was it sent and why? What does it contain? After that, I will point out certain sections of the letter to you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: At that time, Mr. Schwarz-Schilling was the High Representative for Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was from the Federal Republic of Germany, but that doesn't matter much. He invited all of us who had been removed from office pursuant to the decisions of previous high representatives to contact his office for those decisions to be reconsidered and the sanctions possibly abolished. Perhaps my style in this letter was not appropriate and possibly that was why it was never read out to him, but I took that opportunity to tell Mr. Schwarz-Schilling, in brief, that there was not a single reason for that decision of Mr. Ashdown back in 2004 removing me and other colleagues from office, because that happened without establishing the facts prior to that decision. The reason was also because I and some others went about our jobs in the positions to which we were appointed. And finally I said whatever his decision, I would respect it the same way I respected the decision of Mr. Ashdown, although it was totally unjust and unfounded on facts. No investigation was ever launched against us, nor was there a -- a judicial procedure. Only in August of last year, pursuant to a decision by Mr. Intzko, all persons who were suspended with me in 2004 were rehabilitated. However, in the meantime, many things happened that ruined the health and careers of many of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would just like you to look at the second page of this letter sometime -- some place in the middle. In the English version this is at the end of page 1, where it talks about the SDS deputies. I read this letter very carefully, and I can see that you've already testified to this before this Tribunal. All of these facts that you have stated here before this Trial Chamber you also wrote about to the High Representatives as your -- your -- in your role as the president of the Deputies' Club and responsible for liaison with The Hague Tribunal, so we don't really need to state those things again.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Well, again, I said that the decision was made without actual consideration of all the work we did in our co-operation with the Tribunal. When the decision on our replacement was announced, it was said that it was due to our failure to co-operate with The Hague Tribunal, but by that time I had already been to The Hague three times, and I had already referred to the conversation I had with the Prosecution. This was also a topic of discussions before the National Assembly. Simply, this decision was not founded on any facts, simply the High Representative decided to make that decision because we were carrying out certain functions at that time, and I think that there was no other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. To finish this topic, just tell me this, please: Again at one point in time you were summoned by The Hague Tribunal to testify, only this time it was a summons to testify in the case against Radovan Karadzic. Are you able to tell me when this was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: The first contact concerning this case was made in late July by telephone. I think that maybe Mr. Tieger got in touch with me at that time, or one of his associates, I'm not sure, but that's not that important right now. Anyway, he asked me if I was prepared, since two investigators were coming to Sarajevo in late July, whether I was prepared to see them. I said, "No problem at all, Mr. Tieger. We just need to set the place for our meeting." And he also told me the topic that they wanted to discuss with me. The meeting took place in Pale in late July 2009. Knowing, because Mr. Tieger told me what it was all about, I wrote a letter to Mr. Tieger personally, and in the letter I stated some facts that he was probably not aware of, some things that had happened in the meantime, and I told him then about my position that had to do with what was being asked of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, now that you've mentioned that, I would like now in the e-court system to actually show this document but not to broadcast it publicly. That's document D16. Mr. Tupajic, in your binder this is in the -- behind the yellow divider marked with the letter R. Do you see that in front of you? Are you able to see it? Is this your handwriting, can you tell us, and is this the letter that you sent to the OTP of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we can move into private session, please, because now we will discuss certain topics which are not to be discussed in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic. By the way, Mr. Lazarevic, at the outset you said that Mr. Tupajic's testimony would be completed today by the end of working hour. Do you mean that his testimony will last till 3.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. By no means. I believe that we can finish in one hour, maybe an hour and a half. That's a fair estimation, I mean, according to my questions that I drafted, I've already put two-thirds of the questions to Mr. Tupajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lazarevic. But I wanted to let you know we are still -- we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was just about to ask for a private session for one brief moment just in order to finish this topic with Mr. Tupajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tupajic. We'll be in open session for a while to speak about some other facts concerning this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, could you think whether the last answer should remain in private session or a confidential part of transcript or whether that's something that can be discussed in public as well, some part? Shall we go back to -- shall we go back to private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, I wanted to discuss this topic with you anyway, but the Trial Chamber is interested too. Let us go back to the first contacts with the OTP when you were informed that you were to testify before this Tribunal in the Karadzic case. When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: As I said, the first contact was in July 2009, and I spoke about that interview with the OTP representatives at Pale in July. In September, Mr. Tieger called me up and asked me if I was opposed to meeting him in Sarajevo as he would be there briefly at the UN base. Of course, I accepted to meet him, and I met him in the afternoon hours when we spoke for about three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did that conversation take place before you sent the letter to Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: No. It was after that. In late July 2009, I sent the letter to Mr. Tieger through his co-workers. That was -- that's a letter we have already seen here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So after that letter you met again, and what did you speak about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, probably not accepting the reasons I stated in my letter, tried to convince me to come and testify in this case anyway. On that occasion, I tried to convince Mr. Tieger that I had valid reasons for my decision, but I had already stated that in my letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Were there other calls or other meetings with OTP representatives after that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: No. Until July 2011, there were no more contacts. I believe that it was Mr. Tieger who contacted me then, and basically I got a number of instructions from them. I went to Nedzarici, the UN base, to receive the transcripts from my testimony in Krajisnik, and then later they informed me that I didn't have a passport, which was true, because I never needed one in the previous years, and I immediately filed an application for a new passport. And I didn't know how things would develop. I followed all instructions received from the OTP, and I responded to each of their calls.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If we honour the chronology, the next thing that we should mention would be the reception of the subpoena. Did you get the subpoena? What were the circumstances? Where were you? What was happening? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: The first subpoena came in rather late because it was issued on the 23rd of December --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, September, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and I only received it on the 5th of October. I immediately went to the police station where it was handed it me. They make an official note of that fact. I never got a copy though. I then collected medical documentation and sent it to the Trial Chamber asking it to accept the reasons I stated for not being able to respond to the subpoena.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And after that there was another subpoena. Tell us when you got it, how, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: The exact date is stated here. It came in much sooner. At the police station I stated medical reasons, like the first time around, and some other reasons into which I want to go later, I could not act pursuant to the subpoena.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When you received the first and second subpoenas, did you read them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. There was nothing unclear neither in the first or the second subpoena. I was fully aware of all possible consequences. But I also knew that even that would be easier for me to bear than reliving everything I went through after my testimony in 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: After two subpoenas you said you got and understood, the decision was issued to apprehend you and take you to The Hague. How did you get that order?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: Well, that was expected. I actually expected that to happen much earlier. The period from the first subpoena to the arrest warrant was a very stressful period for me. I didn't know all the procedures in force here. For two months or so I was in suspense, but I expected the arrest, and I was aware of what would follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When that came in, did you try to avoid your arrest in any way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: No. Quite to the contrary. The BH authorities know that. I never did anything to indicate that I would oppose my arrest. When they came to arrest me, I told them that I had been waiting for them for quite a while. So I didn't resist my arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, I must ask you this question: You have already testified before the Tribunal in the Krajisnik case. Your state of health at the time was what it was. I don't want to go into the details of it now because we're in open session. You are testifying even now at this moment before this Honourable Trial Chamber. Tell me, what's the difference? How come you can testify today defending yourself but cannot testify in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: I would just like to speak about this in a little more detail now, please, but in view of what I'm going to say, I would kindly ask for that to be done in closed session if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you're asking for that, I think that would be a cautionary measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like ask the Trial Chamber to grant the witness's request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it because it is related to your health condition, Mr. Tupajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What I would like to talk about now has nothing to do with my health condition, but it has to do with the events that ensued after my testimony in the Krajisnik case and on my return to my place of residence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Out of an abundance of caution, we'll grant it. We'll back to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tupajic, for my question and your answer to be given in open session, we must repeat them. I apologise. My last question was, Mr. Tupajic, whether you believe that you failed to respond to the subpoena of this Tribunal without a valid reason.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TUPAJIC
utterances.text: When I made that decision it was a decision that is contrary to my personal codex or to the attitude I embrace in life in general, because I was aware of not acting pursuant to a binding instruction by a Tribunal. But with regard to my state of health and its deterioration in recent times, and given all the unpleasant experiences after my testimony in 2005, as well as my commitments to my family which is in a rather precarious situation, I think that my reasons should be sufficient. Of course, if the Trial Chamber does not accept that, then I'm guilty and I have to accept that. I'm aware of the possibility that my -- the reasons stated will be assessed as insufficient, in which case, I'm willing and ready to accept all consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tupajic. I have no more questions of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, was this evidence given in private session? Do you recollect? I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Well, can we go in private session then? Can we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, shall we deal with the documents you showed during your examination of the accused. You showed 20 documents, starting from D1 to D20.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: From D1 to D20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And among them, if my memory's correct, D16, D20, were discussed in open session, but the others were discussed in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All the others should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So is it your opinion that all the others should remain under seal? I'm particular interested in knowing the status of D17, 18, 19. Those are Mr. Tupajic's letter to MUP, two letters, and one is a stenographical record of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Published on the internet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, as for D19, it can be found on the internet, so there is absolutely no reason for this one to be under seal. However, as for D17 and D18, it's a private letter of Mr. Tupajic, and during his testimony he somehow expressed his disagreement when these letters were sent to the newspapers or made public because they were intended to be sent to just the Ministry of Interior. So maybe out of cautiousness, maybe these two letters should remain under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. How about D7, Mr. Lazarevic? It's the High Representative's decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That one -- that one can be public, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we will admit D7, D16, and D20 publicly, and others will remain admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it you closed your case. There's no further evidence you want to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There is no -- any further evidence. Our case is finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you are going to make a final closing argument, and also, I take it Mr. Tupajic is going to make his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- that's the situation. I am ready to give my closing. Although maybe it would be better if we take a break five minutes earlier to prepare myself for the closing. It won't take more than 15 to 20 minutes for my side and approximately something like that amount of time for Mr. Tupajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would it be okay to have a break for half an hour instead of an hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course, Your Honour. That would be more than sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll take a break about half an hour, and we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. President, a respected colleague of mine while defending before this Tribunal in another contempt case said that there are no minor or small cases, and I completely agree with him. The case in which Mr. Tupajic has been charged for contempt of court did not take long, just one trial day, but nevertheless, it is not a minor or a small case. In volume, it's not a large case. However, it opens some legal and ethical questions on which, of course, this esteemed Trial Chamber will give their opinion in their ruling and the significance of which far exceeds the actual case itself. Mr. Tupajic has been charged after receiving on the 5th of October, 2011, and the 8th of November, 2011, about the content of two subpoenas dated the 23rd of September and the 3rd of November, as well as after being informed of his duty to appear before the Chamber or to state valid reasons due to which he was not able to respond to two subpoenas, has been charged of knowingly and wilfully obstructing the administration of justice because he refused to act upon those subpoenas. Let us now look at the facts of this case. Mr. Tupajic did receive the first and the second subpoena. He was informed about their content and, therefore, was aware of his duty to act pursuant to those subpoenas. This is not in dispute. As for whether Mr. Tupajic wilfully obstructed the administration of justice when he refused to act upon those subpoenas, that is what is at issue here. In my desire to stay as long as possible in open session for my closing arguments, I'm now only going to talk about the fact whether Mr. Tupajic made his decision wilfully. While looking at that, whether he did that wilfully or not, this Trial Chamber needs to keep in mind the following fact: Reaching a wilful decision implies that the person who is making that decision has free will, rather, that there are no reasons which would in any way significantly restrict that individual's free will. I'm going to come back to this topic at some later stage of my closing arguments. Linked to this, of course, is the question of the validity of the reasons Mr. Tupajic cited in his answers relating to the subpoena. The Trial Chamber is familiar with these reasons. They were reviewed in detail in the course of the proceedings, and according to Mr. Tupajic's understanding, these reasons are justified. Before I analyse them in my closing statement, I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber not to look at these reasons one by one, separately, but to view them as a group of circumstances in the case of Mr. Tupajic, because it is not possible to separate each one of them. When we speak about the reasons which led Mr. Tupajic not to act upon the orders of this Trial Chamber, the Trial Chamber would need to ask itself the following questions: Would someone who already testified in a case before this Tribunal refuse to testify again without having a valid reason for doing so? Because the situation of Mr. Tupajic is a specific one. He already testified in the Krajisnik case in 2005. And opposed to somebody who is testifying for the first time, he has first-hand experience about what that means, what it means to testify and what all the aspects of that are. Also, would somebody who in their political endeavours urged the establishment of the co-operation with Republika Srpska with this Tribunal and who actively took part in the adoption of appropriate laws within his jurisdiction without a valid reason refuse to testify before that same Tribunal? Mr. Tupajic testified as to those reasons in his defence, and he was completely sincere before this Trial Chamber. At his explicit request, the Defence did not present any witnesses, and it relied exclusively on written documents considering that they speak for themselves and that the sincere testimony of Mr. Tupajic before this Trial Chamber constitutes his very best defence. If we may now, Your Honours, I would like to move into private session, because now I'm going to be dealing with certain matters that were dealt with previously in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of my closing arguments, I would like to say this: Mr. Tupajic would plead that this Trial Chamber acquit him in this case since the reasons that led him not to act pursuant to orders of this Trial Chamber are valid pursuant to paragraph [as interpreted] 77 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Should this Trial Chamber make a different decision, all the circumstances that were discussed today could be viewed solely as mitigating factors for Mr. Tupajic. The Defence would particularly like to emphasise that Mr. Tupajic is a regular, modest, family man, a man who already testified before this Tribunal and thus gave an important contribution to the work and role of this Tribunal. On the other hand, we believe that there are no aggravating circumstances which could in this case influence the situation of Mr. Tupajic. At the end, I would just like to take this opportunity to thank Mr. Tupajic for the confidence he expressed by allowing me to represent him in his defence. I would also like to thank all the participants in these proceedings who helped to run the whole thing smoothly, and in particular to the interpreters who, as always, have done an exceptionally good job. And I would also like to say that it was my exceptional privilege and pleasure to appear again before this esteemed Trial Chamber. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Lazarevic, does your client wish to make a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, after I had a brief discussion with Mr. Tupajic upon his arrival in the courtroom, he told me that he would -- would like to say just a few words, because he's not really feeling good today, and it was very exhausting for him, and instead of reading what he wrote, he will just like to address the Trial Chamber in just a few words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tupajic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Honourable Chamber, I am quite tired already with the proceedings we've had today, and I will not repeat the issues I've already stated. In my evidence, I have tried to paint a picture of what I have gone through in the past seven or eight years. I don't know how successful I was in doing that. Being a person of technical vocation, I am not given to judging matters relating to words. Let me just emphasise that everything I have stated today is the truth and nothing but the truth. I would like to go back again to the period following my testimony in 2005 to make just one point. I think that I would have endured that period of my life far easier had I been at the UNDU here in The Hague rather than in my place which is Sokolac, and that because of the gravity of what I had to live through. I think that my co-operation with the Prosecution and the Tribunal as a whole did give some sort of contribution to shedding the light and establishing the truth of the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I have always believed that truth will out, and no small role is played in that by the people who give their contribution to that. My contribution to that would have been even greater but for the reasons detailed today by my Defence counsel and myself. I would like to thank both the relevant organs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as the organs here in the Tribunal and the UNDU for what was on their part very decent and correct treatment of me. I trust that Their Honours will thoroughly consider the points I made and that they will render a fair ruling, and whatever the ruling that they may render shall be, I will respect it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please be seated. Thank you, Mr. Tupajic. Very well. The Chamber will consider all the evidence and submissions and deliver the judgement in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I'm not commenting on the merits of the case that we have to determine at all. I simply want to thank you for the very professional and clear way that you conducted this case. It was a pleasure to have that sort of advocacy, which we don't always have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, let me endorse the views of my brother Judge and colleague Judge Morrison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: at 1.28 p.m. sine die
